steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on using conversational language models to coordinate multi-robot systems with a human in the loop. Motivate why multi-robot coordination needs to be flexible, review work on LLM agents that role-play and talk to each other, and briefly present our proof-of-concept system.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Multi-robot systems are spreading; need for flexible, domain-agnostic coordination
2. LLMs as a basis for coordination and communication
3. Role-playing and conversations between multiple LLM agents
4. Applications of role-playing, including robotics
5. Our proof-of-concept system

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Multi-robot systems
- still rare in everyday life, but increasingly common: agriculture, search and rescue, construction
- household robotics market projected to grow considerably this decade -> many robots interacting with users and with each other
- demand for systems that adapt flexibly to new tasks without prior training
- trend towards generalist robotics: same model / overarching structure on many platforms and tasks
- goal: domain-agnostic coordination structure common across platforms; group treated as single entity

2. LLMs
- Large Language Models (LLMs): agents operating on text via next-symbol prediction
- interpret task or agent descriptions; internalised understanding and reasoning
- facilitate communication between agents; control flow stays understandable / accessible to human operator
- multi-modal AI influencing robotics and agent-based research; LLMs power end-to-end approaches using human-written inputs to inform actions
- overarching vision: multimodal, generalist agent operating on text, images, other inputs in robotics

3. Role-playing
- conversational agents like ChatGPT usually model human-agent conversation; some works model conversation between multiple agents
- "role-playing": agent told to "imagine" it is a person with a role, then converses in that role
- internal monologue: single agent "talks to themself" about what it perceives and can do
- multiple personas, each with specialised perspective, editing group solution toward their own goals

4. Applications
- debate; auctions; haggling; checking with human supervisor that not hallucinating
- set conditions for dialogue, let agents talk, assume intelligent solution emerges
- team of software developers writing code, passing responsibilities to next developer
- robotic simulators: communication to organise who performs each task, coordinate workspaces, decide who can reach an object
- agents fetching items in a house: communicate, short-term memory, request assistance on the fly
- diverse skillsets: agents build team with required skills before planning and acting

5. Our system
- proof-of-concept; leverages knowledge of pretrained models; language-based agents talk to each other and to humans in natural language
- discuss and debate strategies -> collaborative solution to high-level mission objective; human supervisor observes or assists
- pipeline: high-level task description -> every step autonomously, from planning to assignment

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Multirobot systems are still fairly rare in everyday life, but they are becoming more and more common in areas like agriculture, search and rescue, and construction. The household robotics market is projected to grow a lot this decade, and this will lead to large numbers of robots that interact not only with their users but also with each other. So there is more and more demand for robotic systems that can adapt flexibly to new tasks without being trained for them first. There is also a recent trend towards generalist robotics, where the same model or overall structure can be deployed on lots of different platforms and tasks. Because of this, we want to move towards a coordination structure that is domain-agnostic and common across platforms, so that the group of robots can be treated as one single entity.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are a popular area of recent development in AI. They are agents that work in the domain of text by predicting the next symbol. LLMs could be a good way to interpret descriptions of tasks or agents, and they can also use their internalised understanding and reasoning to develop the information that is available. LLMs can also allow some degree of communication between agents, which helps them organise, and the control flow stays understandable and accessible to a human operator. Multi-modal AI development is now influencing robotics and other agent-based research fields, using LLMs to power end-to-end approaches that can understand human-written inputs and use them to inform their actions. This is part of a bigger vision of a multimodal, generalist agent that can understand and operate on text, images and other inputs in robotics.

Conversational agents like ChatGPT are usually used to model a conversation between a human and an agent, but some works have looked at modelling a conversation between multiple agents. This is usually done with “role-playing”, where an agent is told to “imagine” that it is a person with a certain role and then it enters a conversation while assuming that role. This can be used to model an internal monologue for a single agent who “talks to themself” about what they can perceive and do. Conversational approaches can also use multiple personas. Each persona brings a different specialised perspective to generating the text together, and they edit the group solution to fulfill the different goals they each have for the end result.

Applications of role-playing
- debate; auctions; haggling; checking with human supervisor that not hallucinating
- set conditions for dialogue, let agents talk, assume intelligent solution emerges
- team of software developers writing code, passing responsibilities to next developer
- robotic simulators: communication to organise who performs each task, coordinate workspaces, decide who can reach an object
- agents fetching items in a house: communicate, short-term memory, request assistance on the fly
- diverse skillsets: agents build team with required skills before planning and acting

Our system
- proof-of-concept; leverages knowledge of pretrained models; language-based agents talk to each other and to humans in natural language
- discuss and debate strategies -> collaborative solution to high-level mission objective; human supervisor observes or assists
- pipeline: high-level task description -> every step autonomously, from planning to assignment

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Multirobot systems are still fairly rare in everyday life, but they are becoming more and more common in areas like agriculture, search and rescue, and construction. The household robotics market is projected to grow a lot this decade, and this will lead to large numbers of robots that interact not only with their users but also with each other. So there is more and more demand for robotic systems that can adapt flexibly to new tasks without being trained for them first. There is also a recent trend towards generalist robotics, where the same model or overall structure can be deployed on lots of different platforms and tasks. Because of this, we want to move towards a coordination structure that is domain-agnostic and common across platforms, so that the group of robots can be treated as one single entity.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are a popular area of recent development in AI. They are agents that work in the domain of text by predicting the next symbol. LLMs could be a good way to interpret descriptions of tasks or agents, and they can also use their internalised understanding and reasoning to develop the information that is available. LLMs can also allow some degree of communication between agents, which helps them organise, and the control flow stays understandable and accessible to a human operator. Multi-modal AI development is now influencing robotics and other agent-based research fields, using LLMs to power end-to-end approaches that can understand human-written inputs and use them to inform their actions. This is part of a bigger vision of a multimodal, generalist agent that can understand and operate on text, images and other inputs in robotics.

Conversational agents like ChatGPT are usually used to model a conversation between a human and an agent, but some works have looked at modelling a conversation between multiple agents. This is usually done with “role-playing”, where an agent is told to “imagine” that it is a person with a certain role and then it enters a conversation while assuming that role. This can be used to model an internal monologue for a single agent who “talks to themself” about what they can perceive and do. Conversational approaches can also use multiple personas. Each persona brings a different specialised perspective to generating the text together, and they edit the group solution to fulfill the different goals they each have for the end result.

Role-playing has been used for many tasks, for example debate, auctions, haggling, and checking with a human supervisor that they are not hallucinating. These approaches set up the conditions for a dialogue and then leave the agents to talk, and they assume that an intelligent solution will come out of the conversation naturally. This has been used to make a team of software developers who each write code and pass responsibilities on to the next developer. LLMs have also been put into robotic simulators for communication to organise who does each task, so that robots can coordinate their workspaces and decide which of them can reach an object. A similar approach simulates agents fetching items in a house, where they communicate and use short-term memory to ask each other for help on the fly. Some works include diverse skillsets where each agent has different capabilities and skills, for example a work where the agents build a team with the skills that are needed before they plan and act.

We present a proof-of-concept system that uses the knowledge of pretrained models by building language-based agents. The agents talk to each other, and to humans, using natural language. This lets the agents discuss and debate their strategies to reach a collaborative solution to a high-level mission objective, and a human supervisor can observe or assist. This makes a pipeline where agents take a high-level task description and do every step of the process autonomously, from planning to assignment.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Multirobot systems, while still fairly rare in everyday life, are becoming increasingly common in domains such as agriculture [1,2], search and rescue [3], and construction [4]. The household robotics market is projected to grow considerably this decade [5], leading to large numbers of robots interacting not only with their users but also with each other. This creates increasing demand for robotic systems which can flexibly adapt to new tasks without prior training. There is also a recent trend towards generalist robotics, where the same model or overarching structure can be deployed on a wide variety of platforms and tasks [6]. To this end, it is desirable to move towards a domain-agnostic coordination structure that is common across platforms, so that the group can be treated as a single entity. Large Language Models (LLMs) [7] are a popular area of recent development in the AI landscape; they are agents that operate in the domain of text through next-symbol prediction. LLMs may be an effective way to interpret task or agent descriptions, and can call on internalised understanding and reasoning to develop the available information. LLMs can also facilitate some degree of communication between agents that helps them organise, while keeping the control flow understandable and accessible to a human operator. Multi-modal AI development is now influencing robotics and other agent-based research fields [8], using LLMs to power end-to-end approaches which can understand and use human-written inputs to inform their actions [9]. This fits into an overarching vision of a multimodal, generalist agent which can understand and operate on text, images, and other inputs in robotics [10]. Although conversational agents such as ChatGPT are typically used to model a human-agent conversation, some works have focused on modelling a conversation between multiple agents. This is typically done through “role-playing”: an agent is told to “imagine” that it is a person with a certain role and then enters a conversation while assuming that role [11]. This process can be used to model the internal monologue of a single agent who “talks to themself” about what they can perceive and do [12]. Conversational approaches can also use multiple personas, each bringing a different specialised perspective to the collective generation of text by editing the group solution to fulfill the different goals they each have for the end result [13].

Role-playing has been used for a variety of tasks including debate [14], auctions, haggling [15,16], and checking with a human supervisor that they are not hallucinating [17]. These approaches set the conditions for a dialogue and leave the agents to talk, assuming that an intelligent solution will emerge naturally from the conversation. This has been used to create a team of software developers who each write code and pass responsibilities on to the next developer [18]. LLMs have also been integrated into robotic simulators for communication to organise who performs each task, allowing robots to coordinate their workspaces and decide which of them can reach an object [19]. A similar approach simulates agents fetching items in a house; they communicate and use short-term memory to request assistance from each other on the fly [20]. Some works include diverse skillsets where each agent has different capabilities and skills, such as one where the agents build a team with the required skills before planning and acting [21].

We present a proof-of-concept system that leverages the knowledge of pretrained models by building language-based agents which talk to each other, and with humans, using natural language. This allows agents to discuss and debate their strategies towards a collaborative solution to a high-level mission objective, with a human supervisor observing or assisting. This forms a pipeline that lets agents take a high-level task description and autonomously perform every step of the process, from planning to assignment.
